difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY - one concept (the sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace) followed by a single-step trigonometric equation $\cos t = 1/\sqrt{2}$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$; about 1-1.5 minutes for a prepared student.
stem:
Let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \gamma_3$ be the eigenvalues of the matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos t & \sin t \\ 0 & -\sin t & \cos t \end{bmatrix},
$$

where $t \in [-\pi, \pi]$ is in radians.

Which one of the following options lists all the possible values of $t$ satisfying $\gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma_3 = 1 + \sqrt{2}$ ?

solution.quick:
The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace: $\gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma_3 = 1 + \cos t + \cos t = 1 + 2\cos t$.

Setting $1 + 2\cos t = 1 + \sqrt{2}$ gives $\cos t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. On $[-\pi, \pi]$ this holds only at $t = \pm\frac{\pi}{4}$: **(C)**.

steps.title: Use trace = sum of eigenvalues
steps.body:
For any square matrix $A$, the sum of its eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity, complex ones included) equals its trace, the sum of the diagonal entries. The diagonal entries here are $1$, $\cos t$ and $\cos t$, so

$$
\gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma_3 = \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1 + \cos t + \cos t = 1 + 2\cos t.
$$

steps.title: Cross-check by finding the eigenvalues explicitly
steps.body:
The matrix is block diagonal: the $1 \times 1$ block $[1]$ and the $2 \times 2$ rotation block $R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \\ -\sin t & \cos t \end{bmatrix}$. So one eigenvalue is $\gamma_1 = 1$. The other two come from

$$
\det(R - \gamma I) = (\cos t - \gamma)^2 + \sin^2 t = \gamma^2 - 2\gamma\cos t + 1 = 0,
$$

which gives $\gamma = \cos t \pm \sqrt{\cos^2 t - 1} = \cos t \pm i \sin t = e^{\pm i t}$.

The sum is $1 + (\cos t + i\sin t) + (\cos t - i\sin t) = 1 + 2\cos t$. The imaginary parts cancel, as the trace rule predicts.

steps.title: Solve the condition
steps.body:
$$
1 + 2\cos t = 1 + \sqrt{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; \cos t = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

The general solution is $t = 2k\pi \pm \frac{\pi}{4}$. Within $[-\pi, \pi]$ only $k = 0$ works, giving

$$
t = \frac{\pi}{4} \quad \text{or} \quad t = -\frac{\pi}{4}.
$$

(For $k = \pm 1$ the values $\pm\frac{7\pi}{4}$ and $\pm\frac{9\pi}{4}$ all lie outside the interval.)

steps.title: Check the options
steps.body:
| $t$ | $\cos t$ | $1 + 2\cos t$ | equals $1 + \sqrt{2} \approx 2.414$? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\pm\pi/4$ | $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$ | $\approx 2.414$ | yes |
| $\pm\pi/3$ | $1/2$ | $2$ | no |

Every option containing $\pm\pi/3$ fails, and $\left\{\frac{\pi}{4}, -\frac{\pi}{4}\right\}$ lists exactly the two solutions. Answer → **(C)**.

solution.teaching:
**Why the trace equals the sum of eigenvalues.** The eigenvalues of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ are the roots of its characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A)$. Expanding the determinant, the only way to get a $\lambda^{n-1}$ term is from the product of the diagonal entries $(\lambda - a_{11})(\lambda - a_{22})\cdots(\lambda - a_{nn})$. So the coefficient of $\lambda^{n-1}$ is $-(a_{11} + \cdots + a_{nn}) = -\operatorname{tr}(A)$. Writing $p(\lambda) = (\lambda - \gamma_1)\cdots(\lambda - \gamma_n)$, the same coefficient is $-(\gamma_1 + \cdots + \gamma_n)$. Comparing the two gives $\sum \gamma_i = \operatorname{tr}(A)$. Comparing constant terms similarly gives $\prod \gamma_i = \det(A)$. Both facts hold even when some eigenvalues are complex.

**Rotation matrices.** A $2 \times 2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \\ -\sin t & \cos t \end{bmatrix}$ rotates the plane by angle $t$ (clockwise, with this sign convention). It is orthogonal ($R^\top R = I$), so all its eigenvalues have modulus 1. Whenever $\sin t \ne 0$ no real direction is left unchanged, so the eigenvalues are the complex pair $e^{\pm i t}$. The given $3 \times 3$ matrix rotates about the first coordinate axis: that axis is fixed (eigenvalue $1$) and the plane perpendicular to it is rotated.

**Block-diagonal matrices.** The eigenvalues of $\begin{bmatrix} B & 0 \\ 0 & C \end{bmatrix}$ are those of $B$ together with those of $C$, because the determinant factors as $\det(B - \lambda I)\det(C - \lambda I)$.

**Connecting to this question.** The condition on the eigenvalue sum is really a condition on the trace, $1 + 2\cos t$. It reduces to $\cos t = 1/\sqrt{2}$, and because cosine is even, the solutions in $[-\pi, \pi]$ come as the symmetric pair $\pm\pi/4$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $t = -\pi/4$ works, but $t = \pi/3$ gives $1 + 2\cos(\pi/3) = 1 + 1 = 2 \ne 1 + \sqrt{2}$. The set also misses the solution $t = \pi/4$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $t = \pi/4$ works, but $t = -\pi/3$ gives $1 + 2\cos(-\pi/3) = 2 \ne 1 + \sqrt{2}$. The set also misses $t = -\pi/4$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\cos(\pm\pi/4) = 1/\sqrt{2}$, so the eigenvalue sum $1 + 2\cos t = 1 + \sqrt{2}$ for both values. These are the only solutions of $\cos t = 1/\sqrt{2}$ in $[-\pi, \pi]$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\cos(\pm\pi/3) = 1/2$, so the eigenvalue sum is $1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac12 = 2$, not $1 + \sqrt{2} \approx 2.414$. Neither value satisfies the condition.

solution.shortcut: Do not compute the eigenvalues. Their sum is the trace, $1 + 2\cos t$, so $\cos t = 1/\sqrt{2}$ and $t = \pm\pi/4$ in one line.
solution.commonTrap: Believing the condition cannot hold because the eigenvalues $e^{\pm i t}$ are complex for $t = \pm\pi/4$. The trace identity counts complex eigenvalues too, and their imaginary parts cancel. A second slip is to use $\sin$ instead of $\cos$, or to drop the eigenvalue $1$ and solve $2\cos t = 1 + \sqrt{2}$, which has no solution because $1 + \sqrt{2} > 2$.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np, sympy as sp
t = sp.symbols('t', real=True)
M = sp.Matrix([[1, 0, 0], [0, sp.cos(t), sp.sin(t)], [0, -sp.sin(t), sp.cos(t)]])
print(sp.factor(M.charpoly().as_expr()), M.eigenvals())   # 1, cos t +/- i sin t
print(sp.simplify(sum(k*v for k, v in M.eigenvals().items())))   # 2*cos(t) + 1 = trace
sols = sp.solveset(sp.Eq(M.trace(), 1 + sp.sqrt(2)), t, sp.Interval(-sp.pi, sp.pi))
print(sols); assert sols == sp.FiniteSet(-sp.pi/4, sp.pi/4)
R = lambda v: np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, np.cos(v), np.sin(v)], [0, -np.sin(v), np.cos(v)]])
for name, vals in {'A': [np.pi/3, -np.pi/4], 'B': [np.pi/4, -np.pi/3], 'C': [np.pi/4, -np.pi/4], 'D': [np.pi/3, -np.pi/3]}.items():
    print(name, [bool(np.isclose(np.linalg.eigvals(R(v)).sum().real, 1 + np.sqrt(2))) for v in vals])   # only C: [True, True]
answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve: the sum of the eigenvalues is the trace, 1 + 2cos t. Setting it equal to 1 + sqrt(2) gives cos t = 1/sqrt(2), so t = +/- pi/4 on [-pi, pi]. sympy gives the eigenvalues as 1 and cos t +/- i sin t, and solveset returns {-pi/4, pi/4}. A numeric eigenvalue check shows that only option C's values both satisfy the condition. This agrees with official key C.
